ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Extension of SEZ facilities 
*321. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Indian apparel Export Units are demanding for extending 
SEZ facilities to their units set up outside SEZ; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that the Government of Andhra Pradesh has requested 
for opening up of SEZ; and 
(d) if so, the details of the request and the action that has been contemplated on that? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI KAMAL 
NATH): (a) and (b) Suggestions have been received for extending facilities such as 
exemption from income tax as available to units in SEZ to apparel export units located 
outside the SEZ. 
(c) and (d) On the basis of proposals received through the Government of Andhra 
Pradesh, approval has been given for setting up of 2 Special Economic Zones in 
Visakhapatnam and Kakinada. The Zone at visakhapatnam is proposed to be 
developed by AP Industrial Infrastructure Corporation Limited while that at Kakinada by the 
Kakinada SEZ Private Limited. 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Sir, the Minister has said that the Indian apparel 
export units have been demanding income-tax exemptions as are available to the units in 
SEZ. Not only income-tax exemptions, but they are also demanding duty-free imports or 
domestic procurement of goods operating outside SEZs apart from other things. 
Therefore, in my 

RAJYASABHA [17 August, 2005] 
first supplementary, I would like to know from the hon. Minister to what 
extent he has succeeded in giving them facilities demanded by the Indian apparel 
export units. May I know whether the Minister can give any time limit, by 
which the SEZs in Visakhapatnam and Kakinada become operational? 
SHRI KAMAL NATH: Sir, the second part first that the Andhra Pradesh 
Industrial Development Corporation has to develop these. They have been 
giving the approval; and the other one in Kakinada is a private party. This is 
really for the State Government to drive it, and, to the extent of the regulatory 
framework, which involves the Stat e Government, where the approval is 
concerned, that has already been given. So, if there is a concern regarding SEZs 
or the developers of the SEZs find any difficulty or need any clarification, the 
Central Government would act immediately. 
The other question relates to apparel units or textile units which have been 
demanding some of the facilities of the SEZs. Sir, the SEZ is a regime of its 
own, it is as per the Act passed by Parliament, by this august House and there is a 
criterion to be an SEZ. We cannot have proliferation of SEZs because SEZ 
envisages a lot of freedom from the regulato.ry framework; it provides more or 
less autonomous structure where customs and other fiscal facilities are 
concerned. So, there have been demands that those who are exporting should 
get some facilities of the SEZs; and to give them level playing field. We cannot 
have a thing called virtual SEZ. Either there is a SEZ or there is no SEZ. SEZ 
is area specific. 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Sir, in my second supplementary, I 
would like to know from the hon. Minister whether it is true that there were 
some policy changes made by the Government in the month of September, 
2004 to give further boost to the units set up by SEZ. If, 'yes', what impact does 
the policy changes have on the export of goods from SEZs in the first half of 
this fiscal? May I know whether these changes are going to be made 
applicable to the units outside SEZs? If not, the reasons may be given. 
SHRI KAMAL NATH: Sir, SEZs have shown very large increase, and, as 
hon. Members are aware, the SEZs fi rst worked under the administrative 
control, worked outside the domain of legal framework. After passing of the 
SEZ Bill by the Parliament, now it is governed under the Act. All the facilities to 
give it a regime of stability.are contained in the 
2 

[17 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
SEZ Act. In fact, the whole object of the SEZ Act was to bring into a legal 
framework various facilities and concessions so that the investors would have 
confidence.That being done so, now the SEZ Act, having been passed by both 
the Houses of Parliament, having been notified, is now operational. So, there is 
now substantial interest and increase in exports of SEZ. The SEZ exports have 
risen year by year. Last year, they have risen by 32 per cent. The exports from 
SEZ have risen by 32 per cent over the previous year. There are 811 units 
operating in SEZ, providing employment to one lakh people. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: That is enough. 
SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, the hon. Minister just said that he is against 
the proliferation of SEZs. But, I understand that there are proposals for around 56 
SEZs on the ground today, So, my question is: Is he diluting the concept of SEZs 
altogether, I mean, is he abandoningthe rigid criteria needed for declaring a 
particular facility in SEZ? Surely, having 56 SEZs and more to come, is making 
a mockery of the concept of SEZ. 
SHRI KAMAL NATH-: Sir, this is not a mockery. This really demonstrates the 
good SEZ policy that we have. If anybody wants to come into the SEZ, if SEZ 
have shown such a remarkable increase in exports, SEZ have a criterion. 
Anybody and everybody cannot come into the SEZ. That is what I was saying. 
SEZ cannot come just in five acres or ten acres. It has a minimum criterion 
which is laid down. An SEZ must have a minimum of 1,000 hectares of land, 
because, unless it has 1,000 hectares, there will be no viability in developing that 
infrastructure. Now, SEZs, which are not product specific, have a minimum 
criterion of 1,000 hectares. Only 47 have been approved. And, we must 
recognise that there are cases where some have been approved and not taken off. 
So, we do anticipate that there will be many proposals by the State Governments, 
from entrepreneurs, from developers to have SEZs because of the success it is 
showing. 
SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Thank you, very much, Sir. I would like to 
know from the hon. Minister, through you, whether the Government is 
thinking of opening up an SEZ in Marathwada region in Maharashtra. It is very 
essential for the development of this backward region. Sir, the request, in this regard, 
has been pending for the last so many years with the Ministry. 
SHRI KAMAL NATH: Sir, the Central Government does not open SEZs. It is 
for the State Government or the private entrepreneurs to open the

SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK: Sir, there is an apprehension in 
the minds of especially the smaller States that economic zones require large 
tracks of land. There is also an apprehen sion that this is an old wine in a new 
bottle. Can the Minister distinguish between the Special Economic Zones 
which were established earlier and the existing Special Economic Zones? What 
is the distinction between the two? 
SHRI KAMAL NATH: Sir, previously, as I said, there was a regime, there 
was a regulatory framework which was not under the law passed by 
Parliament. Obviously, there were facilities which were there in the past. The 
point was to give it an element of stability, to bring it under the legal statute so 
that people would have confidence in it. The Government is apt to change certain 
facilities, certain incentives and certain regulations from time to time. Now that 
there is an Act passed by Parliament, all the supervisory systems, which are laid 
down, are defined in the Act. That is the biggest change which has taken place.

THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI KAMAL

opened only in late 1990s. 
(b) A survey was carried out to explore the feasibility of growing tea in the 
Kishanganj and Araria districts of Bihar. As per its findings, only Kishanganj 
district was found to be suitable for growing tea. 
(c) and (d) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
Suitable steps have been taken by Govenment/Tea Board for assisting the small 
growers' of Kishanganj District in taking up new planting and quality 
improvement. Around 85 growers in Kishanganj district have already 
received subsidy amounting to Rs. 127.56 lakhs for new tea planting. Another 
25 growers have received a sum of Rs. 1.19 lakhs as price subsidy under the 
Price Subsidy Scheme. Under the Quality Upgradation and Product 
Diversification Scheme of the Tea Board, subsidy amounting to Rs. 3.30 lakhs 
has been disbursed during 2004-05 to one B ought Leaf Factory. Further, 
advisory services on maintenance of the young tea plantations are being extended 
to the tea growers through the extension wing of Tea Research Association.

JCO and two other Army personnel moved ahead to investigate. The search 
of the ambush site revealed two fatal and two non-fatal civilian casualties. The 
injured were immediately provided first aid and evacuated to a Field Ambulance. 
One of the injured later succumbed to injuries. On further investigation, it was 
revealed that the casualties were civilians aged between 15 to 18 years and 
residents of Bangargund village. 
31 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2005] 
The area of current incident adjoins the Rajwar forest, which is a traditional 
infiltration route from Keran Sector, leading to the areas in Kupwara region. On 
numerous occasions, the Army had requested the villagers to restrict their movement at 
night, and in case of emergencies, the persons moving were to carry 
lanterns/torches. 
However, the incident has been deeply regretted by the Army. Compensation of 
Rs. three lakhs each to the dead and Rs. two lakhs to the injured civilian has been paid. It is 
pertinent to mention that, the troops deployed in J&K are in a state of perpetual high 
alert, in view of the recent spurt in infiltration attempts by terrorists. To avoid 
repetition of incidents of collateral damage due to mistaken identity, the local population has 
been once again cautioned to strictly follow the instructions under Section 144 and in 
case of emergenices, carry lanterns/torches at night. The Army troops, in turn have been 
sensitized to- exercise restraint and use discretion during conduct of counter terrorist 
operations.

*339. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that in MSEB (Maharashtra State Electricity Board) 
there has been nearly 40 per cent Transmission and Distribution losses and it has 
resulted into a debt of over Rs. 5,000 crore to MSEBT; 
(b) if so, what are the r easons for this huge Transmission and Distribution 
losses and what steps have been taken to ensure that these are brought to the 
minimum nationally acceptable limit; and 
(c) what is the Union Power Ministry's norms in this regard and what 
guidelines are issued to ensure that St ate Electricity Board keep within this 
norm? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) As informed by 
Maharashtra State Electricity Board [p resently known as Maharashtra State 
Electricity Distribution Company Ltd. (MSEDCL)] the transmission and 
distribution (T&D) losses for the year 2004-05 have been estimated at 35.28%. 
This loss includes Technical loss and Non-technical (commercial) loss. 
Although, it is difficult to segregate Technical & Non-Technical (commercial) 
loss, MSEDCL has stated that they are likely to face a shortfall of revenue of 
Rs.2500 crores assuming the technical losses to be about 20% and non-
technical to be 15.28% (10,280 MU of energy). 
(b) In MSEDCL, most of the power is generated by Thermal Power Plants, 
which are located in Eastern part (Vidarbha area) of Maharashtra. The demand 
for electrical power is, however, c oncentrated in central and western 
Maharashtra. All the power generated by the thermal plants is, therefore, 
required to be transmitted to Western Maharashtra over a distance of 600-650 
kms. This results in high losses in Transmission network. Similarly while 
distributing the power to the consumers through its network there is a loss due 
to technical reasons (i.e. heating of conductors etc.) Over a period of time, theft 
of electricity by direct hooking on the LT Lines and tampering of meters etc. have 
been on the rise. The above reasons mainly contribute towards the higher level 
of T&D loss in MSEDCL. 
44 

[17 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
The steps initiated by MSEDCL to reduce the T&D losses are:— 
(i) Erection of new 33/11 KV sub-stations, HT Lines, distribution 
transformers under APDRP Scheme, so as to reduce the overloading at 
all levels thus reducing the technical losses. 
(ii) Providing capacitors on Distribution Transformers in 20 Districts, 
(iii) Distribution Transformer Metering and Energy Accounting, 
(iv) Monitoring the losses in MIDC areas and Express Feeders. 
(v) Detection of theft through flying squads. 
(vi) Establishment of six dedicated po lice stations and three special courts 
for prevention/detection of theft cases and expeditious finalization of 
punishments. 
(vii) High Voltage Distribution System (HVDS) Scheme for theft prone areas being 
implemented to improve HT/LT ratio and thereby reduce the losses. 
(viii) Separate feeders for Gaothans (Habitations) being planned for 4500 
feeders, which will help reduce HT losses. 
(ix) Procurement of distribution transformers having lesser no load losses 
and full load losses. 
(x) System Improvement schemes for establishment of 60 new 33/11 KV 
sub-stations. 
(c). The Government of India ha s launched the Accelerated Power 
Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) with the objective of 
reducing Aggregate Technical and Commercial Losses (AT&C) to a level of 15% 
improving quality of supply of power, increasing revenue collection and 
improving consumer satisfaction. APDRP has been put in place as instrument 
to leverage distribution reforms in the States. Priority is given to projects from 
those States who commit themselves to a time-bound programme of reforms 
as elaborated in the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) and 
Memorandum of Agreement (MoA). Signing of the above documents by the 
State Governments/SEBs/Utilities is a pre-requisite for releasing funds under 
APDRP.

into the allegations of violations of human rights by the Armed Forces as against 
the special procedure prescribed under the Act in such cases, to take 
cognizance of and inquire into allegations of violation of human rights 
notwithstanding the cognizance thereof taken by any other Commission, except 
a Commission appointed under the Commission of Inquiries Act, 1952, 
constitution of Human Rights Courts mandated to dispose off cases within a time 
limit of three months, enabling the Commission to publish its Annual Reports or 
Sepcial Report on expiry of a period of  three months of its receipt in the 
Government even if the Report has not  been placed in Parliament/State 
Legislatures etc. These amendments are being examined keeping in view 
various factors like the objectives of  the Protection of Human Rights Act, 
1993, the role and character of the human rights institutions provided for under 
the Act etc.

Incentives to States producing export quality tea 
† 2353. SHRI HARISH RAWAT: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is any special scheme for giving incentives to the States which 
produce tea suitable for exports; 
(b) the details of assistance being provided to various States under this scheme; 
(c) whether Uttaranchal has sent any proposal for special assistance for revival of old 
areas of tea production and extension of new areas; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) and (b) A new scheme has been 
approved by the Government for providing incentive to the tea producers for producing 
more orthodox teas. This scheme, which became effective from 1st January, 2005 will 
remain in force upto 31st March, 2007. The total outlay earmarked for the schemers 
Rs. 65 crores. 
The scheme is expected to help the industry in changing the product mix to suit the 
demands of the export market. India is essentially a CTC tea producer whereas there is 
greater demand for orthodox tea in the international market. In order to induce the 
producers to produce more orthodox teas, incentive will be given at the rate of Rs. 3 per 
kg for leaf grades and Rs. 2 per kg. for dust grade orthodox teas. An additional subsidy 
at the rate of Rs. 2 per kg. will be provided for the incremental 
volume of orthodox tea produced.

Targets for Indo-Pak trade after SAFTA 
2356. SHRIVI JAY J. DARDA: Will th e Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) what targets have been fixed, over the existing one, the bilateral trade 
between India and Pakistan after introduction of South Asian Free Trade Area 
(SAFTA) from January 1, 2006. 
(b) whether wheat export to Pakistan is also be included over and above the 600 
items which Pakistan is presently importing from India; and 
(c) as Pakistan is presently importing  wheat from Russia, US, etc. on 
comparatively high price, will Government be initiating negotiations in this 
regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) During 2004-05, exports 
from India to Pakistan was valued at US $ 505 million as compared to US $ 
287 million during 2003-04 registering an increase of 76 per cent. During 
2004-05, imports from Pakistan into India was valued at US-$95 million as 
compared to US $ 58 million during 2003-04 showing an increase of 64 per 
cent. 
Under South Asian Free Trade Area Agreement (SAFTA) a phased tariff 
liberalization programme is envisaged. In two years, non-Least Developed 
Contracting States (India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka) will bring down tariffs to 
20% while Least Developed Contracting States 
59 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2005] 
(Bangladesh, Bhutan, Maldives and Nepal) will bring them down to 30%. Non-LDCS will 
then bring down tariffs from 20% to 0-5% in 5 years, while LDCS will do so in 8 years. 
SAFTA is expected to be fully operationalised by 2016. No targets have been fixed for the 
bilateral trade between India and Pakistan after introduction of SAFTA from January 1, 
2006. 
(b) No, Sir. Pakistan has so far allowed 771 items for imports into 
Pakistan from India which do not include wheat. 
(c) During the meeting of two Commerce Ministers of India and Pakistan 
on the sidelines of G-20 Meeting held in March, 2005, India had raised 
the issue of import of wheat by Pakistan from other countries at 
comparatively higher prices and had requested to source the same from 
India at competitive price. The Commerce Minister of Pakistan, while 
noting this request, said that during the last financial year, Pakistan 
produced surplus wheat and, therefore, did not require to import wheat 
from any source.

Feasibility study on FTA with China 
2358. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India and China agreed to undertake a feasibility study on FTA between 
the two countries; 
(b) if so, the details of such feasibility study and the need for it; 
(c) what will be the impact of FTA on the proposal to set up an Asian Economic 
Community; 
(d) whether Government will complete all formalities for the FTA with China 
shortly; and 
(e) the details of advantages to Indian exporters from this FTA with China? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) to (e) During the former Prime 
Minister's visit to China in June, 2003, a Joint Study Group (JSG) comprising 
representatives from India and China was set up to examine the potential 
complementarities between the two countries in expanding trade and economic cooperation. 
The JSG report was submitted to Hon'ble Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and Premier 
Wen Jiabao during the tatter's recent visit to India from 9-12th April, 2005. The JSG 
report recommends an India-China Regional Trading Arrangement, comprising trade in 
goods and services, investments, identified understandings for trade and investment 
promotion and facilitation and measures for promotion of economic cooperation in 
identified sectors. In the Joint Statement released during Premier Wen's visit, the Prime 
Ministers agreed to appoint a Joint Task Force to study in detail the feasibility of and the 
benefits that may derive from the India-China Regional Trading Arrangement 
and give recommendations regarding its content. In view of the above, it is too early to 
assess the advantages to Indian exporters from an FTA with China. At present, there is no 
move to set up an Asian Economic Community.

hygiene assurances to Japan to import indian fruits and nuts;

to presence of certain pests. They had sought vapour heat treatment (VHT) of the 
mangoes to be exported to that country. Necessary equipments for the same was

One time package for tea and coffee/sectors 
2373.   DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
SHRIMATI JAMANA DEVI BARUPAL: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Union Government has approved one time package for tea 
industry and also coffee sectors; 
(b) whether these two schemes of tea and coffee will be implemented by Tea 
Board during the remaining period of Tenth Five Year Plan; 
(c) whether on coffee package CCEA has approved equal sharing of total 
interest burden on special coffee term loans during 3 year moratorium period of 
Rs. 287.1 crore amongst the banks; and 
(d) if so, to what extent this decision will help tea and coffee growers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) to (d) In order to help the tea 
and coffee growers, the Government has recently approved the two packages 
for tea and coffee sectors. 
Package for tea Sector 
The Tea Board would implement the following two schemes during the 
Tenth Plan period, with an outlay of Rs. 93 crores with the funds to be made 
available from the special fund created wi th collections of additional duty of 
excise on tea. 
(i) Grant of subsidy for production of orthodox tea @ Rs.3 per kg for leaf 
grades and Rs 2 per kg for dust grades for existing levels of production with 
additional incentive @ Rsr 2 per kg for the incremental volume over the 
previous year from 1st January 2005 to 31st march 2007 with an outlay of 
Rs. 65 crores. 
(ii) Meeting the actual deficits of  the two research and Development 
Institutions viz. Tea Research Association (TRA) at Tocklai (Assam) and United 
Planters'Association for Southern India-Tea Research Foundation (UPASI-
TRF), Tamil Nadu for a period of five years with effect from 2004-05 subject 
to the maximum of 80% of the expenditure on already agreed items of 
expenditure, of which 49% would be met from the normal Plan outlay of the Tea 
Board and the balance from the special fund. The 
81 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2005] 
outlay for this scheme for a period of five years from 2004-05 i.e from 2004-05 to 
2008-09 would be Rs. 28 crores. 
Package for coffee sector 
With a view to provide relief to coffee growers, Government has approved a 
special relief package to revive coffee sector which envisages the following:- 
(i) Sharing equally the total interest burden on Special Coffee Term  Loan (SCTL) 
during the three year moratorium period of Rs. 287.10 crores amongst the banks, the 
Government and the grower loanees to the extent of one third each. The Government 
Subsidy will be released only after growers had paid their share in full by the end of 
June 2005. 
(ii) To request the banks to lower the interest rates charged on SCTL from the existing 
11% to 9% or rate applicable to agriculture sector whichever is lower, during the 
remaining repayment period of SCTL loans. 
(iii) Writing off coffee developmental loans along with interest amounting to around Rs.24 
crore, due from the Coffee Board to the Government of India. The Coffee Board will 
in turn waive the old developmental loans amounting to around Rs.64.59 crore 
extended by the Board to the coffee growers (below 10 hectares) only. 
(iv) Providing the interest subsidy scheme on working capital loans for small growers 
(below 10 ha) at the rate of 5% and for large growers at rate of 3% for the remaining 
years of the Tenth Plan. However, this subsidy would be reduced by 1% for a 
period of 3 years in the case of those growers who receive the benefit of reduced 
interest burden on SCTL during the moratorium period. 
The above packages are expected to improve tea production and reduce the debt burden 
of coffee growers.

Reforming the functioning of Police 
† 2427. SHRI PYARELAL KHANDELWAL: Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Indian Police is still working under the 1861 Act 
formulated by the Britishers; 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
123 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2005] 
(b) whether it is also a fact that from time to time the Commissions have 
been set up for bringing reforms in functioning of Police; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether it is also a fact that a public interest litigation is pending in the 
Supreme Court for the implementation of recommendations made by 
"Dharam Vira Commission" Set up in this regard; and 
(e) if so, the reaction of Government thereto alongwith details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI SHRIPRAKASH JAISWAL): (a) The Police Act, 1861 is in operation in 
most of the States in the Country. Some States have revised their Police Act. 
(b) and (c) Yes, Sir. The Government of India has set up one Police 
Commission namely the National Police Commission under the Chairmanship 
of Shri Dharam Vira in November, 1977. The Commission subm itted eight 
reports during the period February, 1979 to May 1981 with a number of 
recommendations, which were primarily to be implemented by the State 
Governments. The Reports of the Commission were therefore sent to all the 
State Governments/Union Territory Administrations for consideration and 
implementation. Subsequently, Padmanabhaiah Committee and Malimath 
Committee submitted their reports in 2000 & 2003 which touched upon 
various facets of Police functioning. 
(d) and (e) Yes, Sir. A public interest litigation filed by Shri Prakash Singh 
& Others is pending in the Supreme Court soliciting directions to the Central 
and State Governments with regard to implementation of various 
recommendations of the National Police Commission particularly in the matter 
of selection and fixity of tenure of Director General of Police, formation of State 
Security Commission, separation of investigative work from Law & Order 
functions etc. Central Government through its affidavit, brought to the notice of 
the Apex Court that implementation of most of these important 
recommendations concern the State Governments/Union Territory (UT) 
Administrations and that the State Governments/UT Administrations are being 
pursued regularly for implementation of these recommendations.

Check on foreign funding of anti-national organisations 
2429. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the existing rules and regulations are not sufficient to deal 
with funding of "anti-national" organisations by individual and organisations abroad; 
(b) if so, Government's response thereto; and 
(c) the details of steps taken so far or proposed to be taken for tackling 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
125 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2005] 
overseas funding of anti-national organisations by making stringent and effective rules? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI 
SHRIPRAKASH JAISWAL): (a) to (c) The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 
1976 and the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Rules, 1976 contain adequate provision 
to deal with funding of anti-national organizations by individuals and organizations 
abroad. However, the Government is considering certain changes in the law 
governing the receipt and utilization of foreign contribution by voluntary organizations 
to remove shortcomings noticed in the present law. 
The draft Bill names 'Foreign Contribution (Management and Control) Bill, 2005' as 
was presented to the Cabinet, has been uploaded on the Ministry of Home Affairs 
website: www.mha.nic. for seeking comments/ views of different stakeholders. This 
may be visited to see the salient features of the proposed legislation. The proposed Bill 
has been referred to the Group of Ministers by the Cabinet on 23.6.2005. 
No instances of massive diversion of funds for anti-national activities have come to 
the notice of the Government. Adequate provisions exist in the Foreign Contribution 
(Regulation) Act, 1976, which empower the Central Government to take action against 
foreign contribution recipient organizations, which are found contravening the provision 
of the Act, including acceptance of foreign contribution without registration or prior 
permission, or not properly utilizing it for the stated purposes and objectives. The 
action includes placing the organization in the prior permission category, prohibiting it 
from receiving any foreign contribution, freezing its bank account and prosecuting it in a 
court of law.

Solar and wind energy potential in Rajasthan 
2452. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANJA: Will the Minister of NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that Rajasthan, especially its desert region is endowed 
with high potentiality of Solar and Wind Energy; 
(b) whether any feasibility study has been undertaken by Government to set up Solar 
plants and wind mills to generate power; 
152 

[17 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor; 
(d) whether any Indian/foreign private parties are engaged in harvesting solar and wind 
energy in the region; 
(e) if so, the details thereof, and Government's stake therein; 
(f) whether Government have special schemes/packages to encourage 
tapping of Solar and Wind Energy sources by private individuals; and 
(g) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NON-CONVENTIONAL 
ENERGY SOURCES (SHRI VILAS MUTTEMWAR): (a) Yes, Sir. The desert areas in 
Rajasthan have been found to be suitable for harnessing solar and wind energy potential. The 
level of solar radiation in Rajasthan, especially in the desrt region is estimated at 7 kwh 
per square meter per day during summer, which is high as compared to other parts of 
the country. A total wind power potential of 910 MW has been estimated in Rajasthan, 
out of which a potential of 600 MW is available in desert areas. 
(b) and (c) yes, Sir. Based on the feasibility study undertaken by the State 
Government, a proposal has been formulated for installation of an integrated solar 
combined cycle power generation project of 140 MW capacity, consisting of 35 
MW based on solar and 105 MW based on conventional fuel, by Rajasthan 
Renewable Energy Corporation Limited at Mathania district Jodhpur. Based on 
wind resource assessments carried out at 36 locations in Rajasthan, 6 potential 
sites for installation of wind power projects have been identified at Devgarh 
(district Chittorgarh), Harshnath (district Sikar), Jaisalmer, (district Jaisalmer), 
Mohangarh (district Jaisalmer), Khodal (district Barmer) and Phalodi (district 
Jodhpur). 
(d) and (e) There is no foreign firm engaged in harvesting/harnessing solar and wind 
energy in the region. The ownership integrated solar combined cycle power 
generation project is solely with the State Government and the Central Government's 
role is limited to provision of a grant of Rs.50 crore. Wind turbines are being manufactured 
and set up by two private Indian firms, one of which is having foreign collaboration with 
a company in Europe. There is no Government stake in these firms. 
153 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2005]

individuals for usign solar and wind energy. However, incentives such as 
subsidy, accelerated depreciation, co ncessional duty on import of raw 
materials and certain products/component excise duty exemption on certain 
devices/systems are provided by the Government to promote solar and wind 
energy systems.

Electronic meters 
2456. SHRI VEDPRAKASH P. GOYAL: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the new electronic meter installed by power 
companies are manipulated by companies in their favour; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether any comparative study has been done regarding increase in 
power bills after installation of electronic meter; and 
(d) if so, what are findings, give details? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) to (d) Section 55 
of the Electricity Act, 2003 provides that no licensee shall supply electricity 
exept through installation of a correct meter in accordance with the regulations 
made in this behalf by the Central Electricity Authority (CEA). Further, State 
Electricity Regulatory Commissions are required to specify an Electricity 
Supply Code under section 50 of the Act. Contravention of regulations is a 
punishable offence as per the provisions of the Act. 
Electronic meters read all the el ectricity consumption including the 
electricity consumed by a zero watt bulb (6 to 12 watts). These meters record 
the consumption of the electronic gadgets even when they are in stand by mode 
while the mechanical meters are unable to record this consumption because of 
their higher tolerance limit. Mechanical meters tend to get slower with the 
passage of time because of wear and tear in the measuring components. 
The Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission has informed that there have 
been consumers' complaints regarding inaccurate readings after installation of 
Electronic meters. The DERC and also  the Distribution Companies have 
separately conducted meter-testing drives. The latest drive conducted by the 
Distribution Companies was in associ ation with Central Power Research 
Institute (CPRI), an autonomous body of the Ministry of Power, Government 
of India. The results from this drive show that 515 meters have been tested in 
the presence of CPRI in the areas of BSES Yamuna Power Ltd. and BSES 
Rajdhani Power Ltd. (till mid June 2005) and all meters were found to be 
within limits. As regards the area of North Delhi Power Ltd., 45 meters have 
been tested till the end of 
157 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2005] 
July 2005 and all meters were found to be within limits excepting one which 
was found to be slow.

Effect of reduced discharge of water flow on power generation 
2470. DR. K. KASTURIRANGAN: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is reduced discharge across Sutlej, Beas 
and Yamuna Basins, that is resulting in reduced power generation in the recent 
years; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether Government has any plans to augment the water flow to enable 
power houses to operate their optimal capacity; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) The inflows in 
Sutlej during the years 2000-01, 2001-02, 2004-05 and in Beas during the year 
2002-03, 2003-04 and 2004-05 have been less and below dependable year 
inflows. The available flow data for river Yamuna does not clearly indicate 
natural reduction in the flow of river Yamuna. During the year 2004-05 
discharge in Yamuna basin was on a lower side than the discharge available in 
the previous year. The reduction in inflows has resulted in reduced power 
generation. However, inflows in Sutlej and Beas during the current year 
2005-06 so far have been very good. Consequently the generation has also 
been higher than the previous year. 
(b) Inflows in the rivers are contributed by snow melt and rains. The 
reduced inflows in the above mentioned years has been due to less rains/ snow 
fall in the catchment area. 
(c) and (d) Hydro Electric St ations are either of run-of-river type or 
storage type. Generation in run-of-river power stations depends upon the 
discharge available in the river and there is either no pondage or very less 
pondage available. As such, generation in such plants would depend mainly on 
the inflows which in turn depends upon rainfall/snowfall in the catchment area 
of these stations. Reservoir based stations enable water to be stored in the 
monsoon period which could be utilised during lean period of the year. 
Government is having plans to construct both types of stations depending upon 
water availability and topography of the site. 
171 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2005] 
In Sutlej basin, Bhakra (1325 MW) is a reservoir based station in operation 
and Khab Storage scheme (636 MW) is under investigation. In Beas basin, Pong 
(396 MW) is a reservoir based station in operation. In Yamuna Basin, Lakhwar-
vyasi (420 MW), Kishau (600 MW) and Renuka (40 MW) are the planned 
reservoir based projects. The water flow from reservoir schemes can be 
regulated to enable power houses to operate to their optimal capacity.

Information regarding faulty digital meters 
Orissa Electricity Regulatory Commission 
A specific case has been registered by the consumers against CESCO in case No. 
7/2003 dated 11.9.2003 and the Commission after thorough scrutiny and hearing both 
the parties directed as under:— 
"In the persent scenario aggressive metering is highly required to check the rising trend 
of distribution losses. So, any effort by any Distribution Licensee for a mega-metering 
project is most welcome. There is no doubt that CESCO's effort to replace the 
existing defective meters with better quality meter is appreciable. The Commission 
was also given to understand by CESCO that around 80,000 meters have been 
installed so far in various areas under CESCO and not a single complaint from a 
genuine consumer has been received relating to the newly installed meter. The report of the 
Chief Elelctrical Inspector revealed that all these meters confirm to the permissible 
limits as stipulated in IS-13010-1990. The special features of the electromechanical 
meter are polycarbonate case and magnetic suspension bearing with high level of 
accuracy under various conditions of load. The transparent case makes it easy for 
detection of any tampering. 
In the above circumstances, the Commission considers that the general apprehension of 
the consumers/general public about the accurate reading of these Chinese meters is 
untenable. However, in case of any individual compliant, the respondent licensee should 
act promptly to do the needful." 
Punjab State Electricity Regulatory Commission 
There is a general feeling amongst the consumers that the digital meters are 
faster and unreliable. The Board, on the other hand, feels that the digital meters are 
accurate and not so easily tampered whereas mechanical meters tend to get slower 
with the passage of time and are easily tampered and as such the digital meters are 
resisted by the consumers. However, no detailed and reliable studies have been 
conducted by the Board in this regard and as such it is not possible to say that the 
digital meters are actually faulty or unreliable.
